1.title: Variables, Objects, Dynamic Typing and type()
1.html:
Source: Chat 01 “Learn Python Variables” – Lesson 1

Question: Variables as names pointing to objects; dynamic typing; type() – teach me this in ASD-STE100.
Learning format: ASD-STE100 | Level: Beginner | Goal: Read and understand Python code used in GenAI engineering.

What will you learn?

After this lesson, you will be able to:

  • Create Python variables.
  • Understand how variable names point to objects.
  • Understand dynamic typing.
  • Use type() to check the type of an object.
  • Read these concepts in AI agent and RAG code.

First, understand a variable

A variable is a name that refers to an object.

Think of Python as a room with objects. Each object has a value. A variable gives you a name that you can use to access that object.

Example

Python
name = "Python"
  • name → the variable name.
  • "Python" → a string object.

The name name refers to the string object "Python".

Read the code

Python
name = "Python"
  • name is the variable name.
  • = assigns a reference to the object.
  • "Python" is a string object.
Important: In Python, = does not mean mathematical equality. It assigns a value or reference to a name.

Variables can refer to different objects

Look at this code.

Python
x = 10
x = 20

What happens?

  • x = 10 → the name x refers to the object 10.
  • x = 20 → the name x now refers to the object 20.

After the second assignment, x refers to 20. It no longer refers to 10.

Run this code mentally:

Python
x = 10
x = 20

print(x)
Output
20

Python does not need you to create a new variable name every time the value changes.

What is dynamic typing?

Python uses dynamic typing.

This means a variable name can refer to objects of different types at different times.

Example:

Python
x = 10
x = "Hello"
x = 3.14

Here is what happens.

StatementObject type
x = 10int
x = "Hello"str
x = 3.14float

Python allows these assignments.

Why? Because the type belongs to the object, not permanently to the variable name.

Compare Python with this simplified idea of a statically typed language:

Python
# Python
x = 10
x = "Hello"  # Valid

Python accepts the second assignment. A statically typed language may reject a similar change when the variable is declared as an integer.

Remember: Dynamic typing does not mean that Python has no types. Every object still has a type.

What does type() do?

The built-in function type() tells you the type of an object.

Example:

Python
age = 23
print(type(age))
Output
<class 'int'>

Python tells you that the object referred to by age is an integer.

Here are common types.

ExampleMeaningType
age = 23Whole numberint
price = 99.5Decimal numberfloat
name = "Uma"Textstr
is_ready = TrueTrue or Falsebool
items = [1, 2, 3]Collection of itemslist
config = {"model": "LLM"}Key-value collectiondict
result = NoneNo value is availableNoneType

Try this example:

Python
model = "sarvam"
temperature = 0.2
messages = ["Hello", "How are you?"]

print(type(model))
print(type(temperature))
print(type(messages))
Output
<class 'str'>
<class 'float'>
<class 'list'>

This is useful when you inspect data from an API, a model, a database, or an AI agent.

Why does this matter in GenAI engineering?

Suppose you are writing a simple AI agent.

Python
user_query = "Explain RAG"
context = ["Document A", "Document B"]
temperature = 0.2

print(type(user_query))
print(type(context))
print(type(temperature))

You get:

  • user_query refers to a string.
  • context refers to a list.
  • temperature refers to a float.

These types matter because different operations work with different types.

For example:

Python
user_query = "Explain RAG"

print(user_query.upper())
Output
EXPLAIN RAG

But this will fail:

Python
user_query = 123

print(user_query.upper())

Why? The integer object does not have the string method .upper().

Engineering rule: When code fails unexpectedly, check the type of the value first.
Python
print(type(user_query))

This simple check can help you debug agent inputs, tool outputs, retrieval results, and API responses.

Interactive practice

Predict the output before you reveal the answer.

Question 1: What does this print?

Python
x = 5
x = "AI"
print(x)

Options: 5 / AI / An error

Question 2: What does type(score) return?

Python
score = 98.5
print(type(score))

Options: <class 'int'> / <class 'str'> / <class 'float'>

Question 3: Which statement is correct?

Options: A variable name has one permanent type. / Python objects have types, and a name can refer to objects of different types. / Python does not use types.

Show the answer

1 – AI (the name now refers to the string). 2 – <class 'float'>. 3 – Python objects have types, and a name can refer to objects of different types.

Your coding task

Write this code in Python, then run it.

Python
model = "qwen"
tokens = 150
temperature = 0.7
is_running = True

print(type(model))
print(type(tokens))
print(type(temperature))
print(type(is_running))

Your goal is to identify each object type without looking at the table above.

Lesson summary

  • Variable: A name that refers to an object.
  • Object: A value stored and managed by Python.
  • Assignment (=): Makes a name refer to an object.
  • Dynamic typing: A name can refer to objects of different types at different times.
  • type(): Returns the type of an object.

One final distinction: x = 10 does not permanently make x an integer. It makes x refer to the integer object 10 at that point in the program.

2.title: Data Types – int, float, str, bool, None
2.html:
Source: Chat 01 “Learn Python Variables” – Lesson 2

Question: Data types: int, float, str, bool, None – teach me this in ASD-STE100.

Learning objective

After this lesson, you will be able to:

  • Identify int, float, str, bool, and None.
  • Select the correct data type for a value.
  • Use type() to check a value's type.
  • Understand how data types affect Python code.
  • Recognize these types in AI agents, APIs, and RAG pipelines.

What is a data type?

A data type tells Python what kind of value an object represents.

For example, 25 is a number. "Hello" is text. True is a Boolean value.

Think of data types as different kinds of containers. Each type supports different operations.

Example valueTypeMeaning
123intWhole number
3.14floatDecimal number
"Hello"strText
TrueboolTrue or False
NoneNoneTypeRepresents the absence of a value

Learn each data type

A. int: Integer

An integer is a whole number. It does not contain a decimal point.

Python
age = 23
tokens = 150
temperature = -5

print(type(age))
Output
<class 'int'>

Use int for:

  • Number of students.
  • Number of API requests.
  • Token counts when you represent them as whole numbers.
  • Loop counters.
Remember: 23 is an integer. 23.0 is a float.

B. float: Floating-point number

A float represents a number that can contain a decimal part.

Python
price = 99.5
temperature = 0.7
score = 85.25

print(type(temperature))
Output
<class 'float'>

Use float for:

  • Model temperature settings.
  • Similarity scores.
  • Measurements.
  • Decimal calculations.

Example from GenAI:

Python
similarity_score = 0.87

if similarity_score > 0.8:
    print("Relevant document")

The condition checks whether the score is greater than 0.8.

Important: Python floats use binary floating-point representation. Some decimal values cannot be represented exactly.

C. str: String

A string represents text.

You can use single quotes or double quotes.

Python
name = "Python"
message = 'Learn AI engineering'
model = "sarvam"

print(type(model))
Output
<class 'str'>

Use str for:

  • User questions.
  • AI model names.
  • Prompts.
  • API messages.
  • Document content.

Example:

Python
user_query = "Explain agentic RAG"

print(user_query.upper())
Output
EXPLAIN AGENTIC RAG

Notice the difference:

Python
a = 25
b = "25"

print(type(a))
print(type(b))
Output
<class 'int'>
<class 'str'>

The first value is a number. The second value is text.

Python does not automatically treat them as the same type.

D. bool: Boolean

A Boolean represents one of two values:

  • True
  • False

Both values start with a capital letter in Python.

Python
is_logged_in = True
has_api_key = False

print(type(is_logged_in))
Output
<class 'bool'>

Use bool for:

  • Checking whether a user is logged in.
  • Checking whether a task is complete.
  • Checking whether an API request succeeded.
  • Controlling if statements.

Example:

Python
is_agent_ready = True

if is_agent_ready:
    print("Start the agent")
else:
    print("Wait for configuration")
Output
Start the agent

Python executes the first branch because is_agent_ready is True.

E. None: No value

None represents the absence of a value.

It is not the same as 0, False, or an empty string.

Python
result = None

print(result)
print(type(result))
Output
None
<class 'NoneType'>

Use None when:

  • A result is not available yet.
  • A search returns no result.
  • A function does not return a meaningful value.
  • You need to represent a missing optional value.

Example:

Python
answer = None

if answer is None:
    print("No answer is available")
Output
No answer is available

Use is None to check for None.

Compare the five types

ValueTypeMeaning
42intWhole number
42.0floatDecimal number
"42"strText
TrueboolBoolean value
NoneNoneTypeNo value

A common beginner error is to confuse a value with its type.

For example, "False" is a string. It is not the Boolean value False.

Interactive practice

Predict the result before you check the answer.

1. What is the type of 100?

Options: float / int / str

2. What is the type of "0.5"?

Options: float / str / bool

3. Which value represents no value?

Options: 0 / False / None

4. What is the type of 0.5?

Options: int / float / str

5. Which value is a Boolean?

Options: "True" / True / "False"

Show the answer

1 – int. 2 – str (it is in quotes). 3 – None. 4 – float. 5 – True (without quotes).

Apply these types to an AI agent

Consider this example:

Python
user_query = "Explain RAG"
max_tokens = 500
temperature = 0.2
is_streaming = True
answer = None

print(type(user_query))
print(type(max_tokens))
print(type(temperature))
print(type(is_streaming))
print(type(answer))

The output is:

Output
<class 'str'>
<class 'int'>
<class 'float'>
<class 'bool'>
<class 'NoneType'>

These types have different purposes:

  • user_query stores text.
  • max_tokens stores a whole-number limit.
  • temperature stores a decimal setting.
  • is_streaming stores a true-or-false setting.
  • answer indicates that no answer is available yet.

This is a simplified example. A real model API may use different parameter names and validation rules.

Your coding task

Write the code and predict the output.

Python
model = "qwen"
attempts = 3
score = 0.95
success = True
error = None

# Add five print(type(...)) statements here.

Your task is to print the type of every variable.

Then change attempts to "three" and check its type again. Python permits the assignment because it uses dynamic typing.

Lesson checklist

  • I can identify an integer.
  • I can identify a float.
  • I can identify a string.
  • I can identify a Boolean.
  • I can explain the meaning of None.
  • I can use type() to check a value.

3.title: Operators – Arithmetic, Comparison and Logical
3.html:
Source: Chat 01 “Learn Python Variables” – Lesson 3

Question: Operators: / vs //, %, **, comparison, logical.

Learning objective

After this lesson, you will be able to:

  • Use arithmetic operators to calculate values.
  • Explain the difference between / and //.
  • Use % to calculate a remainder.
  • Use ** to calculate a power.
  • Compare two values.
  • Use logical operators to combine conditions.
  • Apply these operators in AI agent code.

What is an operator?

An operator tells Python to perform an operation on one or more values.

For example:

Python
total = 10 + 5

Here:

  • 10 and 5 are values.
  • + is an operator.
  • total refers to the result, 15.

Think of operators as tools in your coding toolbox. Each tool has a different job.

Arithmetic operators

OperatorNameWhat it doesExample
/DivisionDivide two numbers. The result is normally a float.7 / 2 → 3.5
//Floor divisionRound the quotient down to the nearest whole-number value, or lower integer.7 // 2 → 3
%ModuloReturn the remainder from division.7 % 2 → 1
**ExponentiationRaise a number to a power.2 ** 3 → 8

A. / versus //

Suppose you have 7 tokens to distribute equally between 2 groups.

  • / gives the exact division result.
  • // gives the floor of the division result.
Python
print(7 / 2)
print(7 // 2)
Output
3.5
3
Important: // does not always mean that Python removes the decimal part. It rounds down toward negative infinity.

For example:

Python
print(-7 // 2)
Output
-4

The mathematical result is -3.5. The next lower integer is -4.

B. %: Remainder

Use % to find what remains after division.

Python
print(10 % 3)
print(12 % 2)
Output
1
0

Why?

  • 10 divided by 3 leaves a remainder of 1.
  • 12 divided by 2 leaves a remainder of 0.

A common use is to check whether a number is even.

Python
number = 8

if number % 2 == 0:
    print("Even")
else:
    print("Odd")
Output
Even

C. **: Power

The ** operator raises a number to a power.

Python
print(2 ** 3)
print(5 ** 2)
Output
8
25

This means:

  • 2 ** 3 is 2 × 2 × 2.
  • 5 ** 2 is 5 × 5.

Do not confuse ** with ^. In Python, ^ performs bitwise XOR, not exponentiation.

Comparison operators

Comparison operators compare two values. Python returns a Boolean result: True or False.

OperatorMeaningExampleResult
==Equal to5 == 5True
!=Not equal to5 != 3True
>Greater than8 > 5True
<Less than2 < 1False
>=Greater than or equal to5 >= 5True
<=Less than or equal to3 <= 5True

Understand = versus ==

This distinction is important.

Python
age = 23       # Assign a value
print(age == 23)  # Compare two values
Output
True
  • = assigns a value to a name.
  • == checks whether two values are equal.

Example from an AI application:

Python
status = "success"

print(status == "success")
Output
True

The comparison checks whether the status is "success".

Logical operators

Logical operators combine conditions or change a Boolean result.

Python has three main logical operators:

and

Both conditions must be true.

Python
print(True and True)    # True
print(True and False)   # False

or

At least one condition must be true.

Python
print(True or False)    # True
print(False or False)   # False

not

Reverse the truth value.

Python
print(not True)   # False
print(not False)  # True

Example: AI agent access

Suppose an AI tool requires a valid API key and an active account.

Python
has_api_key = True
account_active = True

if has_api_key and account_active:
    print("Tool access allowed")
Output
Tool access allowed

If either condition is False, the combined condition is False.

Now consider an application that accepts two types of input:

Python
is_text_query = True
is_voice_query = False

if is_text_query or is_voice_query:
    print("Accept the query")

The query is accepted because at least one condition is True.

Truth table for and, or and not

The interactive truth-table explorer in the chat showed how the three logical operators change the result. Here is the complete table:

ABA and BA or Bnot A
TrueTrueTrueTrueFalse
TrueFalseFalseTrueFalse
FalseTrueFalseTrueTrue
FalseFalseFalseFalseTrue

Combine comparison and logical operators

This is where operators become useful in real programs.

Python
similarity = 0.92
document_found = True

if similarity >= 0.8 and document_found:
    print("Use the document")
else:
    print("Search for more information")

The program checks two conditions:

1. Is the similarity score at least 0.8?

2. Was a document found?

Both conditions must be true to use the document.

This is a simplified example of a decision rule in a RAG pipeline. Real retrieval systems need more than a similarity threshold to determine whether a document is useful.

Knowledge check

1. What is the result of 7 / 2?

Options: 3 / 3.5 / 1

2. What is the result of 7 % 2?

Options: 3 / 3.5 / 1

3. What is the result of 2 ** 4?

Options: 8 / 16 / 6

4. When is A and B true?

Options: When either condition is true / When both conditions are true / When both conditions are false

5. What is the result of not False?

Options: False / None / True

Show the answer

1 – 3.5. 2 – 1. 3 – 16. 4 – When both conditions are true. 5 – True.

Lesson summary

OperatorPurposeExample
/Normal division7 / 2 → 3.5
//Floor division7 // 2 → 3
%Remainder7 % 2 → 1
**Power2 ** 3 → 8
==Check equality5 == 5 → True
!=Check inequality5 != 3 → True
> / <Compare values8 > 5 → True
andBoth conditionsTrue and False → False
orAt least one conditionTrue or False → True
notReverse truth valuenot True → False

Your practice task: Write a small Python program that checks whether a document has a similarity score of at least 0.8, whether a document exists, and whether the program should use it.

4.title: Type Conversion – int(), float(), str(), bool()
4.html:
Source: Chat 01 “Learn Python Variables” – Lesson 4

Question: Type conversion: int(), float(), str(), bool().

Learning objective

After this lesson, you will be able to:

  • Convert a value from one data type to another.
  • Use int(), float(), str(), and bool().
  • Identify values that Python cannot convert.
  • Avoid common type-conversion errors.
  • Convert data that you receive from users, APIs, and AI tools.

What is type conversion?

Type conversion changes a value from one data type to another.

For example, a user enters their age as text:

Python
age = "23"

Python treats "23" as a string. You cannot always use it as a number.

Convert it to an integer:

Python
age = int("23")

print(age + 1)
Output
24

The int() function converts the string "23" to the integer 23.

Think of type conversion as a translator. It changes a value into a form that your code can use.

Meet the four conversion functions

FunctionConverts toExampleUseful for
int()An integerint("25") # 25Whole-number input
float()A floatfloat("3.5") # 3.5Decimal values
str()Textstr(25) # "25"Messages and text formatting
bool()A Booleanbool(1) # TrueChecking truth values

Learn int()

The int() function converts a suitable value to an integer.

Python
age = int("23")
score = int(90.8)

print(age)
print(score)
Output
23
90

Notice that int(90.8) produces 90. It removes the fractional part. It does not round to the nearest integer.

Values that work

Python
int("42")    # 42
int(7.9)     # 7
int(-3.8)    # -3
int(True)    # 1
int(False)   # 0

Values that fail

Python
int("hello")

Python raises a ValueError because "hello" is not a valid integer representation.

Also, int("3.5") raises a ValueError. Convert the string to a float first if that is your intended operation:

Python
int(float("3.5"))  # 3

Learn float()

The float() function converts a suitable value to a floating-point number.

Python
temperature = float("0.7")
score = float(10)

print(temperature)
print(score)
Output
0.7
10.0

Examples:

Python
float("3.14")  # 3.14
float(5)       # 5.0
float(True)    # 1.0
float(False)   # 0.0

This conversion fails:

Python
float("hello")

Python raises a ValueError because the text does not represent a valid number.

Learn str()

The str() function converts a value to its string representation.

Python
age = 23
message = "My age is " + str(age)

print(message)
Output
My age is 23

Without str(age), this expression raises a TypeError:

Python
"My age is " + 23

Python does not automatically combine a string and an integer with +.

More examples:

Python
str(3.14)   # "3.14"
str(True)   # "True"
str(None)   # "None"
Important: str(None) produces the text "None". It does not produce the special value None.

Learn bool()

The bool() function converts a value to True or False.

Python treats some values as false (falsy): False, None, 0, 0.0, "" and empty collections such as [] and {}. The complete list of truthy and falsy values is in Chapter 5.

Most other values are true, including non-empty strings and non-zero numbers.

Python
print(bool(0))
print(bool(1))
print(bool(""))
print(bool("False"))
print(bool(None))
Output
False
True
False
True
False

The surprising result is bool("False"), which returns True.

Why? Because "False" is a non-empty string. Python checks whether the string is empty, not whether the text describes a false value.

  • bool("") → False. The string is empty.
  • bool("False") → True. The string contains six characters.

Do not use bool() to parse text such as "true" or "false" from an API. Use explicit validation instead.

For example:

Python
enabled_text = "false"

enabled = enabled_text.lower() == "true"

print(enabled)
Output
False

Apply type conversion to a GenAI project

Suppose your application receives user settings as text.

Python
user_input = "0.7"
temperature = float(user_input)

if temperature <= 1.0:
    print("Temperature is within the selected limit")

The application converts the text to a number before it compares the value.

This is important when you process API inputs, configuration values, and tool outputs.

Handle conversion errors safely

User input may contain invalid data. Do not assume that every value can be converted.

Python
user_input = "twenty"

try:
    age = int(user_input)
    print(age)
except ValueError:
    print("Enter a valid whole number.")
Output
Enter a valid whole number.

The try block runs the conversion. The except block handles the ValueError if the conversion fails.

In production code, also validate limits and allowed values. A successful conversion does not mean the input is valid for your application.

Knowledge check

1. What does int(8.9) return?

Options: 9 / 8 / 8.9

2. What does float("5") return?

Options: 5.0 / "5" / An error

3. What does str(True) return?

Options: 1 / True as a Boolean / "True" as a string

4. What does bool("False") return in Python?

Options: False / True / None

5. What happens when int("hello") runs?

Options: Returns 0 / Returns None / Raises ValueError

Show the answer

1 – 8 (the fractional part is removed, not rounded). 2 – 5.0. 3 – "True" as a string. 4 – True. 5 – Raises ValueError.

Lesson summary

FunctionPurposeExample
int()Convert to integerint("25") → 25
float()Convert to floatfloat("3.5") → 3.5
str()Convert to stringstr(25) → "25"
bool()Check truthinessbool("") → False

Before you continue, remember these three rules:

1. Conversion can fail. Handle invalid input.

2. Conversion can change the value. For example, int(8.9) returns 8.

3. A Boolean conversion checks truthiness. It does not interpret text as a Boolean word.

5.title: Truthy and Falsy Values; is vs ==
5.html:
Source: Chat 10 “Truthy Falsy Comparison Guide” (turn 1); comparison example merged from Chat 11 (turn 3)

Question: Truthy and falsy values; is vs == – in ASD-STE100.

What are truthy and falsy values?

Python checks if a value is true or false in a condition.

  • Truthy: Python treats the value as True.
  • Falsy: Python treats the value as False.

You do not need to convert every value to True or False. Python checks the value for you.

Common falsy values

ValueDescriptionTruth value
0, 0.0Number zeroFalsy
""Empty stringFalsy
[], {}, (), set()Empty collectionsFalsy
False, NoneOther falsy valuesFalsy

Most other values are truthy. For example:

  • 1
  • -5
  • "hello"
  • "False"
  • [1, 2, 3]
  • {"name": "Uma"}
Important: "False" is a non-empty string. It is truthy. False is a Boolean value. It is falsy.

How does Python use these values?

Consider an AI chatbot that receives a user's question.

Python
question = "Explain RAG"

if question:
    print("Process the question")
else:
    print("Ask for a question")
Output
Process the question

Python checks whether question is empty.

  • If the string contains text, Python treats it as truthy.
  • If the string is "", Python treats it as falsy.

You can also write this:

Python
question = ""

if not question:
    print("Please enter a question")
Output
Please enter a question

Here, not reverses the truth value.

Try it yourself: what does bool(value) return?

Predict the result for each value before you read the table. (In the chat this was an interactive selector.)

ExpressionResultWhy
bool([])FalseAn empty list is falsy.
bool([0])TrueThe list is not empty; it contains one item.
bool(0)FalseZero is falsy.
bool("0")TrueA non-empty string is truthy.
bool(None)FalseNone is falsy.
bool("False")TrueA non-empty string is truthy (see Chapter 4).
bool({})FalseAn empty dictionary is falsy.

== versus is

Both operators compare things. However, they answer different questions.

  • == checks whether two objects have equal values.
  • is checks whether two references point to the same object.

Example 1: Use == to compare values

Python
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = [1, 2, 3]

print(a == b)
Output
True

Both lists contain the same values in the same order.

Example 2: Use is to compare identity

Python
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = [1, 2, 3]

print(a is b)
Output
False

Python created two separate list objects. Their contents are equal, but the objects are different.

In short: a == b → True (same contents); a is b → False (different objects).

Example 3: Both operators return True

Python
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a

print(a == b)
print(a is b)
Output
True
True

Here, b = a makes b refer to the same list object as a.

Example 4: compare a shared reference and an equal copy

Example:

Python
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a
c = [1, 2, 3]

print(a == b)
print(a is b)

print(a == c)
print(a is c)
Output
True
True
True
False

Explanation:

  • a and b refer to the same list.
  • a and c refer to different lists.
  • The lists have equal contents, so a == c is True.
  • They are different objects, so a is c is False.

Rules for everyday Python:

  • Use == to compare values.
  • Use is None to check whether a value is None.
  • Use is for object identity only when you need to know whether two references point to the same object.

When should you use is?

The most important case is checking for None.

Python
response = None

if response is None:
    print("No response received")
Output
No response received

Use is None and is not None when you want to check for None.

Python
if response is not None:
    print("Response received")

Why does this matter in AI engineering?

An AI function may return None when it has no result. You can check this before you process the result.

Python
def retrieve_document():
    return None

document = retrieve_document()

if document is None:
    print("No document found")
else:
    print("Process the document")

Do not write if not document when you specifically need to detect None. An empty string, an empty list, and zero are also falsy.

Important difference: None, False, 0 and ""

These values are all falsy, but they are not the same value.

Python
print(None == False)  # False
print(0 == False)     # True
print("" == False)    # False

print(None is None)   # True
print(False is False) # True

Why does 0 == False return True? Python treats Boolean values as a subtype of integers. False has the numeric value 0, and True has the numeric value 1.

However, 0 is False is False. The integer zero and the Boolean False are different objects.

Common mistakes

Incorrect or risky codeBetter codeReason
if value == None:if value is None:Check identity with None.
if value is "hello":if value == "hello":Compare string contents.
if len(items) > 0:if items:Check whether a collection is non-empty.
if not response:if response is None:Use this when only None means missing.

Avoid using is to compare ordinary numbers, strings, or list contents. Python may reuse some immutable objects, so identity results for such values can be surprising.

Quick knowledge test

1. What is the truth value of an empty dictionary {}?

Options: Truthy / Falsy

2. What does == check?

Options: Object identity / Value equality

3. What does is check?

Options: Object identity / Whether values look equal

4. What is the recommended way to check if result is None?

Options: result == False / result is None

5. What is bool("False")?

Options: False / True

Show the answer

1 – Falsy. 2 – Value equality. 3 – Object identity. 4 – result is None. 5 – True.

Remember these four rules

1. Truthy: Python treats the value as True in a condition.

2. Falsy: Python treats the value as False in a condition.

3. ==: Compare values.

4. is: Compare object identity. Use is None to check for None.

These rules are useful when you build Python functions, RAG pipelines, LLM applications, and AI agents.

How does Python use these values?

6.title: Strings – Slicing, split, join, strip, replace, f-strings and Prompts
6.html:
Source: Chat 01 “Learn Python Variables” – Lesson 5

Question: Strings: slicing, split, join, strip, replace, f-strings, multi-line strings (prompts are strings).

Learning objective

After this lesson, you will be able to:

  • Extract part of a string with slicing.
  • Split a string into smaller parts.
  • Join strings together.
  • Remove unwanted spaces with strip().
  • Replace text with replace().
  • Insert variables into f-strings.
  • Write multi-line strings for AI prompts.

Why this matters: Prompts, user questions, retrieved documents, tool results, and model responses are often strings. You need to know how to process them.

What is a string?

A string is a sequence of characters. Python uses the str type for strings.

Python
name = "Python"
prompt = "Explain how RAG works"

You can access, search, split, and modify string content.

Meet a string

The string "PYTHON" has six characters. Python starts counting at index 0.

CharacterPYTHON
Index012345
Negative index-6-5-4-3-2-1

Index 0 points to P. Index 1 points to Y. Index 5 points to N.

String slicing: [:]

Slicing extracts part of a string.

Syntax:

Python
text[start:stop:step]
  • start is the index where Python starts.
  • stop is the index where Python stops. Python does not include this index.
  • step is the number of positions to move each time. It is optional.

Example:

Python
text = "PYTHON"

print(text[0:3])
print(text[2:5])
print(text[:3])
print(text[3:])
Output
PYT
THO
PYT
HON

Notice that text[0:3] returns indexes 0, 1, and 2. It does not include index 3.

You can also use negative indexes.

Python
text = "PYTHON"

print(text[-1])
print(text[-3:])
Output
N
HON

-1 refers to the last character.

split(): Divide a string

The split() method divides a string into a list of smaller strings.

Example:

Python
text = "Python AI Agents"

words = text.split()

print(words)
Output
['Python', 'AI', 'Agents']

By default, split() separates the text at whitespace.

You can also specify a separator.

Python
skills = "Python,SQL,RAG,Agents"

print(skills.split(","))
Output
['Python', 'SQL', 'RAG', 'Agents']

When can you use it?

You can split a comma-separated list of skills, words in a sentence, or simple text records.

Remember: split() returns a list, not a string.

join(): Combine strings

The join() method combines strings from an iterable, such as a list.

Example:

Python
words = ["Python", "AI", "Agents"]

result = " ".join(words)

print(result)
Output
Python AI Agents

The string before .join() defines the separator.

Python
words = ["Python", "SQL", "RAG"]

print(", ".join(words))
print(" | ".join(words))
print("".join(words))
Output
Python, SQL, RAG
Python | SQL | RAG
PythonSQLRAG
Important: The list items must be strings. This code fails:
Python
numbers = [1, 2, 3]

print(", ".join(numbers))

Convert the numbers first:

Python
numbers = [1, 2, 3]

result = ", ".join(str(n) for n in numbers)

print(result)
Output
1, 2, 3

split() and join() work together

"Python,AI,RAG" → .split(",") creates a list → ["Python", "AI", "RAG"] → " ".join(...) combines the list items → Python AI RAG

strip(): Remove unwanted spaces

The strip() method removes whitespace from the beginning and end of a string.

Example:

Python
query = "   Explain RAG   "

print(query.strip())
Output
Explain RAG

There are three useful methods:

MethodWhat it removes
strip()Both ends
lstrip()Left side
rstrip()Right side

Example:

Python
text = "   Python   "

print(text.strip())
print(text.lstrip())
print(text.rstrip())
Output
Python
Python   
   Python

Whitespace includes spaces, tabs, and newline characters.

GenAI use case: Clean unwanted whitespace from a user query before you send it to a retrieval system or model.

Python
user_query = "   Explain agentic RAG   "
clean_query = user_query.strip()

Note that strip() does not remove spaces inside the text.

"Explain agentic RAG" remains unchanged.

replace(): Replace text

The replace() method returns a new string with matching text replaced.

Syntax:

Python
text.replace(old, new)

Example:

Python
text = "I use Java"

result = text.replace("Java", "Python")

print(result)
Output
I use Python

You can also set a replacement limit.

Python
text = "AI AI AI"

print(text.replace("AI", "ML", 2))
Output
ML ML AI

Python replaces the first two occurrences.

Important: Strings are immutable. replace() does not change the original string.
Python
text = "Hello"
text.replace("Hello", "Hi")

print(text)
Output
Hello

To keep the result, assign it to a variable:

Python
text = text.replace("Hello", "Hi")

Use replace() for simple text changes. Do not use it as a complete solution for removing sensitive information or safely parsing complex formats.

F-strings: Insert variables into text

An f-string lets you insert variables or expressions into a string.

Place f before the opening quotation mark. Then place each variable or expression inside {}.

Example:

Python
name = "Uma"
skill = "GenAI"

message = f"My name is {name}. I learn {skill}."

print(message)
Output
My name is Uma. I learn GenAI.

You can also include calculations.

Python
a = 10
b = 5

print(f"Total: {a + b}")
Output
Total: 15

You can format decimal values, too.

Python
score = 0.87654

print(f"Score: {score:.2f}")
Output
Score: 0.88

Here, .2f displays two digits after the decimal point.

Multi-line strings: Write text on several lines

A multi-line string can contain several lines of text.

Python uses triple quotes for this:

  • """ ... """
  • ''' ... '''

Example:

Python
prompt = """
You are a Python tutor.
Explain concepts in simple words.
Give one example.
Ask one practice question.
"""

print(prompt)

The string contains all four lines.

You can also create a multi-line string without triple quotes by using \n for newline characters. Triple quotes are often easier to read for long text.

Why are multi-line strings important for GenAI?

An AI prompt often contains instructions, context, examples, and an expected output format.

You can store the entire prompt in one string.

Python
role = "Python tutor"
topic = "string slicing"

prompt = f"""
Role: {role}

Task:
Explain {topic} to a beginner.

Rules:
- Use simple words.
- Give one Python example.
- Explain the output.
- Ask one practice question.
"""

print(prompt)

This is a prompt string. The f-string inserts the values of role and topic.

The prompt is now easier to edit and maintain.

Prompt anatomy

SectionExample text
ROLEYou are a Python tutor.
TASKExplain string slicing.
RULESUse simple words. Give an example. Explain the output.

These are sections inside one string. Python does not treat them as separate instructions automatically. Your application sends the prompt to the model.

Important: Triple quotes do not automatically create a special prompt type

This code:

Python
prompt = """Explain RAG.
Give an example."""

creates a normal string (str).

It does not automatically call an AI model. Your code must pass the string to a model API or another component.

Also, triple-quoted strings can preserve leading spaces and newline characters. Format your prompt carefully.

Knowledge check

1. What does "PYTHON"[0:3] return?

Options: PYT / PYTH / YTH

2. What does "a,b,c".split(",") return?

Options: "a b c" / ['a', 'b', 'c'] / ['a,b,c']

3. Which expression combines list items with spaces?

Options: " ".join(words) / words.strip() / words.replace()

4. What does " AI ".strip() return?

Options: " AI " / "AI" / " A I "

5. How do you insert a variable into a string using an f-string?

Options: "Hello, (name)" / f"Hello, {name}" / "Hello, " + {name}

6. What type is a triple-quoted prompt?

Options: prompt / list / str

Show the answer

1 – PYT. 2 – ['a', 'b', 'c']. 3 – " ".join(words). 4 – "AI". 5 – f"Hello, {name}". 6 – str.

Lesson summary

OperationPurposeExample
SlicingExtract part of a stringtext[0:3]
split()Convert a string to a list"a,b".split(",")
join()Combine strings" ".join(words)
strip()Remove whitespace at both endstext.strip()
replace()Replace matching texttext.replace("AI", "ML")
F-stringInsert values into textf"Hello, {name}"
Triple quotesWrite multi-line stringsprompt = """..."""

Your practical task

Create a multi-line prompt for a Python tutor. Include the topic in a variable. Use an f-string to insert that topic into the prompt. Then use strip() to remove unwanted whitespace from a sample user question.

When you can do this without looking at the examples, you are ready to use string operations in basic AI agent workflows.
toc: Multi-line strings: Write text on several lines

7.title: Control Flow – if/elif/else, for, while, break, continue, for…else
7.html:
Source: Chat 11 “Python Collections Guide” (turn 7)

Question: Control flow: if/elif/else, for, while, break, continue, for ... else.

What is control flow?

Control flow decides which code runs and when it runs.

Without control flow, Python runs statements in order, from top to bottom.

Control flow lets your program:

  • Make decisions.
  • Repeat tasks.
  • Stop a loop.
  • Skip an iteration.
  • Run code when a loop finishes without finding a match.

Think about an AI agent. It may need to check a user's request, choose a tool, and repeat a search until it finds a useful answer. Control flow makes these actions possible.

if, elif, and else: Make decisions

Imagine your AI agent receives a request. It must decide what action to take.

Use if, elif, and else to select a path.

Python
score = 85

if score >= 90:
    print("Excellent")
elif score >= 70:
    print("Good")
else:
    print("Keep practicing")
Correction: the chat's version of this example assigned scored = 85 but tested score; that would raise a NameError. The variable name is corrected here.
Output
Good

How does Python decide?

1. Is score >= 90? No → check the next condition.

2. Is score >= 70? Yes → the condition is true, so Python prints Good.

The code follows these rules:

  • if checks the first condition.
  • elif checks another condition if the earlier condition was false.
  • else runs when all earlier conditions were false.
  • Python runs only the first matching branch in this chain.

Important: Indentation

Python uses indentation to identify which statements belong to a condition.

Python
temperature = 35

if temperature > 30:
    print("It is hot")
    print("Drink water")

print("Program finished")

Both indented statements belong to the if block. The final statement runs regardless of the condition.

Use four spaces for each indentation level.

AI engineering example

Python
user_request = "calculate and search for Python tutorials"

if "search" in user_request:
    print("Use the search tool")
elif "calculate" in user_request:
    print("Use the calculator")
else:
    print("Ask an LLM to handle the request")

This is a simple rule-based example. Real AI agents may use model-generated tool decisions, but Python control flow still determines how the application handles those decisions.

for: Repeat for each item

Use a for loop when you want to process each item in a collection.

Example:

Python
tools = ["search", "python", "database"]

for tool in tools:
    print(tool)
Output
search
python
database

Read this line:

Python
for tool in tools:

It means:

1. Get the first item from tools.

2. Assign that item to tool.

3. Run the indented code.

4. Repeat for the next item.

5. Stop when there are no more items.

The variable tool holds one item at a time.

Use range() to repeat a task

Python
for number in range(5):
    print(number)
Output
0
1
2
3
4

range(5) produces the sequence of integers from 0 to 4. The number 5 is not included.

You can specify a starting value:

Python
for number in range(1, 6):
    print(number)
Output
1
2
3
4
5

AI engineering example

Imagine that a RAG pipeline retrieves three documents. You need to inspect each document.

Python
documents = [
    {"text": "Python basics", "score": 0.95},
    {"text": "Python lists", "score": 0.82},
    {"text": "Python loops", "score": 0.76}
]

for document in documents:
    print(document["text"])

The loop processes each dictionary. You do not need to write separate code for every document.

while: Repeat while a condition is true

Use a while loop when repetition depends on a condition.

Python
attempts = 0

while attempts < 3:
    print("Trying...")
    attempts += 1
Output
Trying...
Trying...
Trying...

Here is what happens:

  • Python checks whether attempts < 3.
  • If the condition is true, Python runs the loop.
  • attempts += 1 increases the value by one.
  • Python checks the condition again.
  • The loop stops when the condition becomes false.

The statement attempts += 1 is important. Without it, attempts stays at 0, and the loop continues forever.

for vs while

forwhile
Processes items in a collectionRepeats while a condition is true
Often used when the items are knownOften used when the stopping point depends on a condition
Can use range() for repeated stepsNeeds a condition that can eventually become false, unless another statement stops it

Both loops can solve many of the same problems. Choose the one that makes your code easier to understand.

AI engineering example

An agent may retry a request when an operation fails.

Python
attempts = 0
max_attempts = 3

while attempts < max_attempts:
    attempts += 1
    print(f"Attempt {attempts}")

This demonstrates a retry counter. A real application must also check whether the operation succeeded and decide when to stop retrying.

break: Stop the loop immediately

Use break when you want to exit a loop before it finishes normally.

Example:

Python
for number in range(1, 6):
    if number == 3:
        break

    print(number)
Output
1
2

When number becomes 3, Python executes break. The loop stops immediately. Python does not process 4 or 5.

AI engineering example

Stop searching when you find a sufficiently relevant document.

Python
documents = [
    {"name": "Doc A", "score": 0.55},
    {"name": "Doc B", "score": 0.91},
    {"name": "Doc C", "score": 0.80}
]

for document in documents:
    if document["score"] >= 0.90:
        print("Found:", document["name"])
        break
Output
Found: Doc B
Important: break stops the loop. It does not stop the entire Python program.

continue: Skip the current iteration

Use continue when you want to skip the rest of the current loop iteration and move to the next one.

Example:

Python
for number in range(1, 6):
    if number == 3:
        continue

    print(number)
Output
1
2
4
5

When number is 3, Python skips print(number). The loop continues with 4.

Compare break and continue

StatementWhat it doesExample use
breakStop the entire loop.Stop searching when you find the required result.
continueSkip the current iteration.Ignore an invalid document and process the next document.

AI engineering example

Python
scores = [0.91, -1, 0.82, 0.95]

for score in scores:
    if score < 0:
        continue

    print(score)
Output
0.91
0.82
0.95

The loop ignores the invalid negative score and processes the remaining values.

for ... else: Run code when the loop finishes without break

This feature often confuses beginners. Let's make it simple.

A for ... else statement has two parts:

  • for processes the items.
  • else runs if the loop finishes without executing break.

Example:

Python
numbers = [2, 4, 6, 8]

for number in numbers:
    if number % 2 != 0:
        print("Odd number found")
        break
else:
    print("No odd numbers found")
Output
No odd numbers found

Every number is even. The loop finishes without break, so Python runs the else block.

Now change the list:

Python
numbers = [2, 4, 7, 8]

for number in numbers:
    if number % 2 != 0:
        print("Odd number found:", number)
        break
else:
    print("No odd numbers found")
Output
Odd number found: 7

The loop executes break. Therefore, the else block does not run.

Process each item → Did the loop execute break? Yes → skip else. No → run else.

Important: for ... else does not mean "run else when the if condition is false." It means "run else when the loop completes without break."

AI engineering example: Search for a document

Python
documents = ["Python basics", "RAG guide", "Agent guide"]
target = "SQL guide"

for document in documents:
    if document == target:
        print("Document found")
        break
else:
    print("Document not found")
Output
Document not found

This pattern is useful for searches. It lets you handle the case where no item matches.

The same rule applies to while ... else: the else block runs if the loop finishes without break.

Practice by doing

Predict the output of each program. Select your answer to check your understanding.

1. What does this print?

Python
for i in range(4):
    if i == 2:
        break
    print(i)

Options: 0, 1 / 0, 1, 3 / 0, 1, 2

2. Which numbers are printed?

Python
for i in range(4):
    if i == 2:
        continue
    print(i)

Options: 0, 1 / 0, 1, 3 / 0, 1, 2, 3

3. When does a for-loop's else block run?

Python
for item in items:
    if item == target:
        break
else:
    print('Not found')

Options: Every time the loop ends / Only when the target is found / When the loop finishes without break

4. What happens here?

Python
x = 0
while x < 3:
    x += 1
print(x)

Options: 2 / 3 / Infinite loop

Show the answer

1 – 0, 1. 2 – 0, 1, 3. 3 – When the loop finishes without break. 4 – 3 (the loop stops when x reaches 3).

Your final revision sheet

KeywordPurpose
ifCheck a condition
elifCheck another condition
elseRun the alternative branch
forProcess items one by one
whileRepeat while a condition is true
breakStop the loop
continueSkip the current iteration
for ... elseRun else if the loop finishes without break

Your AI engineering takeaway: These statements control how your application makes decisions, processes data, handles retries, and searches for results. Learn to predict which statement runs next. That skill will make complex Python agent code much easier to read.
toc: if, elif, and else: Make decisions
while: Repeat while a condition is true
for ... else: Run code when the loop finishes without break

8.title: Collections – list, tuple, dict, set and Time Complexity
8.html:
Source: Chat 01 “Learn Python Variables” – Lesson 6, merged with Chat 11 “Python Collections Guide” (turn 1). Both chats taught this topic; the two lessons are combined here.

Question: Collections: list, tuple, dict, set, when to use each, time complexity (asked in both chats).

Learning objective

After this lesson, you will be able to:

  • Explain list, tuple, dict, and set.
  • Select the correct collection for a task.
  • Add, remove, and access items.
  • Understand time complexity.
  • Use collections in AI agents, RAG systems, and APIs.

What is a collection?

A collection stores multiple values in one object.

Suppose you build an AI agent. You may need to store:

  • A list of conversation messages.
  • A fixed set of configuration values.
  • A mapping between model names and settings.
  • A collection of unique document IDs.

Python provides four useful collection types.

CollectionSyntaxMain propertyExample
list[ ]Ordered and changeable. Stores items in sequence. Allows duplicates.messages = ["Hi", "Hello", "Help"]
tuple( )Ordered and immutable. Keeps a sequence that you cannot change in place. Items can repeat.point = (10, 20)
dict{key: value}Key-value mapping. Looks up a value by its key.config = {"model": "qwen", "temp": 0.2}
set{ }Unique elements. Removes duplicates and supports fast membership tests on average.skills = {"Python", "RAG", "Python"}
Remember these four questions:

1. Do you need an ordered sequence that can change? Use a list.

2. Do you need a sequence that cannot change in place? Use a tuple.

3. Do you need to look up values by keys? Use a dict.

4. Do you need unique elements? Use a set.

list: Store a sequence of items

A list stores multiple items in a defined order.

You can change a list after you create it.

Python
messages = ["Hello", "Explain RAG", "Thanks"]

print(messages[0])
Output
Hello

Python uses zero-based indexing. The first item has index 0.

Common list operations

Python
messages = ["Hello", "Explain RAG"]

messages.append("Thanks")
print(messages)

messages.remove("Hello")
print(messages)
Output
['Hello', 'Explain RAG', 'Thanks']
['Explain RAG', 'Thanks']

Use append() to add an item at the end. Use remove() to remove the first matching value.

Other useful operations:

Python
messages[0]       # Access first item
len(messages)     # Count items
messages.pop()    # Remove and return last item
"Hello" in messages  # Check membership

GenAI example: Store conversation messages or retrieved documents in a list.

Python
retrieved_docs = [
    "Document about RAG",
    "Document about embeddings",
    "Document about retrieval"
]

Key rules for lists:

  • Use square brackets: [].
  • Items have positions called indexes.
  • The first index is 0.
  • Duplicate items are allowed.
  • You can change the items.

Another example – add, remove and read tools:

Python
tools = ["search", "python", "browser"]

tools.append("calculator")
print(tools)

tools.remove("browser")
print(tools)

print(tools[0])
Output
['search', 'python', 'browser', 'calculator']
['search', 'python', 'calculator']
search

AI example: Store the tools available to an agent.

Python
agent_tools = ["search", "python", "database"]

tuple: Store a fixed sequence

A tuple is ordered, like a list. However, you cannot replace, add, or remove its items in place.

Python
coordinates = (10, 20)

print(coordinates[0])
Output
10

This fails:

Python
coordinates[0] = 15

Python raises a TypeError.

Use a tuple when you want to represent a fixed group of values.

Python
model_limits = (1000, 0.7)

Here, the tuple may represent a token limit and a temperature setting.

AI example: Store a fixed pair of coordinates or a fixed configuration.

Python
image_size = (1024, 768)
Important: A tuple is immutable, but an object inside it may still be mutable. For example, a tuple can contain a list that you can modify.

A one-item tuple requires a comma:

Python
one_item = (10,)

Without the comma, (10) is just an integer inside parentheses.

Key rules for tuples:

  • Use parentheses: ().
  • Items have indexes.
  • Duplicate items are allowed.
  • You cannot replace, add, or remove tuple items through normal item operations.

Another example – a tuple cannot be changed in place:

Python
coordinates = (10, 20)

print(coordinates[0])
print(coordinates[1])
Output
10
20

This does not work:

Python
coordinates[0] = 50

Python raises a TypeError because a tuple does not support item assignment.

Important: A tuple is not automatically deeply immutable. If it contains a mutable object, such as a list, that inner object can still change.

dict: Store key-value pairs

A dictionary stores data as keys and values.

Think of a dictionary as a labelled cabinet. You use a key to find its value.

Python
config = {
    "model": "qwen",
    "temperature": 0.2,
    "max_tokens": 500
}

print(config["model"])
Output
qwen

Here:

  • "model" is a key.
  • "qwen" is its value.
  • "temperature" and "max_tokens" are also keys.

Change a value

Python
config["temperature"] = 0.5
config["stream"] = True

The first line updates an existing value. The second line adds a new key-value pair.

Common dictionary operations

Python
config["model"]          # Get a value
config.get("timeout")    # Get a value safely if missing
config.keys()            # Get keys
config.values()          # Get values
config.items()           # Get key-value pairs
"model" in config        # Check whether a key exists

Use get() when a key may not exist:

Python
timeout = config.get("timeout", 30)

If "timeout" is missing, timeout becomes 30.

By contrast, config["timeout"] raises a KeyError if the key does not exist.

GenAI example: Store model settings, parsed JSON responses, or metadata for retrieved documents.

Python
document = {
    "id": "doc_101",
    "text": "RAG combines retrieval and generation.",
    "score": 0.91
}

print(document["score"])
Output
0.91

Key rules for dictionaries:

  • Use curly braces: {}.
  • Store each item as key: value.
  • Keys must be unique.
  • Values can repeat.
  • Dictionaries preserve insertion order in modern Python.
  • Use user["name"] to retrieve a value by key.

Another example – read, update and add values:

Python
user = {
    "name": "Ravi",
    "age": 23,
    "role": "AI Engineer"
}

print(user["name"])
print(user["role"])
Output
Ravi
AI Engineer

You can update or add values:

Python
user["age"] = 24
user["city"] = "Hyderabad"

AI example: Store the configuration for an AI agent.

Python
agent_config = {
    "model": "my-model",
    "temperature": 0.2,
    "max_tokens": 1000
}
Note: Accessing a missing key with user["email"] raises a KeyError. Use user.get("email") when a missing key is possible.

set: Store unique elements

A set stores unique elements. It does not provide index-based access like a list.

Python
skills = {"Python", "RAG", "Python", "Agents"}

print(len(skills))
Output
3

The duplicate "Python" is stored only once.

Set elements have no guaranteed positional order that you should rely on.

Common set operations

Python
skills = {"Python", "RAG"}

skills.add("Agents")
skills.discard("RAG")

print("Python" in skills)
Output
True

Use add() to add an element. Use discard() to remove an element without raising an error if it is missing.

Compare two sets

Python
a = {"Python", "RAG"}
b = {"RAG", "Agents"}

print(a | b)  # Union
print(a & b)  # Intersection
print(a - b)  # Difference

Conceptually:

  • Union: all unique elements from both sets.
  • Intersection: elements shared by both sets.
  • Difference: elements in a that are not in b.

GenAI example: Remove duplicate document IDs or track unique skills.

Python
document_ids = ["d1", "d2", "d1", "d3", "d2"]
unique_ids = set(document_ids)

print(len(unique_ids))
Output
3
Remember: use a set when uniqueness matters. Do not use it when you need to preserve the original order or count duplicate occurrences.

Key rules for sets:

  • Use curly braces with comma-separated values: {1, 2, 3}.
  • Duplicate values are removed.
  • Sets do not support indexing.
  • Sets are unordered.
  • An empty set uses set(), not {}. Empty {} creates a dictionary.

Another example – duplicates are removed; add items and check membership:

Python
document_ids = {101, 102, 102, 103}

print(document_ids)

Output contains only three unique values:

Output
{101, 102, 103}

The display order is not guaranteed.

You can add items and check membership:

Python
document_ids.add(104)

print(102 in document_ids)
print(999 in document_ids)
Output
True
False

AI example: Remove duplicate document IDs from retrieval results.

Python
retrieved_ids = [101, 102, 101, 103, 102]
unique_ids = set(retrieved_ids)

print(unique_ids)

Compare the four collections

Featurelisttupledictset
Syntax[](){key: value}{value}
OrderedYesYesYes, insertion orderNo
DuplicatesYesYesKeys: noNo
Change itemsYesNoYesYes
Access by indexYesYesNoNo
Find by keyNoNoYesNo
Best useChanging sequenceFixed sequenceNamed valuesUnique values

Time complexity: How fast are collections?

Time complexity describes how the work required by an operation changes as the number of items increases.

Let n represent the number of items in a collection.

For example, a collection may contain 10 items, 1,000 items, or 1 million items.

We use Big O notation to describe this growth.

Three common complexity classes

NotationNameMeaningExample
O(1)Constant timeThe operation takes approximately the same amount of work as the collection grows.Accessing a list item by index.
O(n)Linear timeThe work can grow in proportion to the number of items.Searching a list for a value.
O(n²)Quadratic timeThe work can grow with the square of the number of items.Comparing every pair of items with nested loops.

These are growth rates, not exact running times. Real performance also depends on the operation, the data, and the computer.

Complexity of common collection operations

The following are typical average-case costs for Python's built-in collections. Worst-case behavior can differ.

Operationlisttupledictset
Access by indexO(1)O(1)Not applicableNot applicable
Lookup by keyNot applicableNot applicableO(1) avg.Not applicable
Membership testO(n)O(n)O(1) avg.O(1) avg.
Append / addO(1) amortizedNot supportedN/AO(1) avg.
Insert at beginningO(n)Not supportedN/AN/A
Remove an arbitrary itemO(n)Not supportedO(1) avg. by keyO(1) avg.
Iterate over all itemsO(n)O(n)O(n)O(n)

Notes:

  • dict and set use hash tables. Their average lookup and membership costs are O(1), but worst-case costs can be O(n).
  • list.append() is O(1) amortized. Some appends require Python to allocate more storage.
  • Removing a list item by value requires a search and may require shifting other items.
  • A tuple has no append or remove method. Creating a modified tuple requires creating a new tuple.
  • A dictionary is a mapping, so it uses keys rather than numeric positions to retrieve values.
  • Dictionary and set deletion costs assume the key or value is already known.

Why does the difference matter?

Consider a list with 1,000,000 document IDs.

Python
document_ids = list(range(1_000_000))

print(999_999 in document_ids)

Python may check many items before it finds the value. The search has O(n) time complexity.

Now use a set:

Python
document_ids = set(range(1_000_000))

print(999_999 in document_ids)

A set uses a hash table. Membership checks usually take O(1) average time.

For repeated membership checks, a set can be much faster than a list. The trade-off is that a set uses extra memory and does not preserve a usable item index.

Use a set when you need repeated membership checks and do not need duplicate entries or index-based access.

Use a dictionary when you need to retrieve metadata by document ID:

Python
documents = {
    "doc1": {"score": 0.92, "text": "RAG basics"},
    "doc2": {"score": 0.87, "text": "Embedding basics"}
}

print(documents["doc1"]["score"])

This pattern is useful for looking up document metadata, tool configuration, and cached results.

Choose the correct collection

CollectionUse it whenTypical AI-engineering usesExample
listOrder matters and items can change or contain duplicates.Conversation history, message sequences, retrieved documents, ordered tool results.messages = ["What is Python?", "Explain a list"]
tupleYou need an ordered sequence that cannot change in place.Coordinates, coordinate pairs, fixed ranges, values that should not be reassigned.chunk_range = (100, 200)
dictEach value has a name or key that you retrieve it by.Model configuration, API responses, JSON data, structured agent state.result = {"answer": "Python uses indentation.", "score": 0.95}
setValues must be unique, or you make repeated membership checks.Unique document IDs, deduplication, visited nodes, checking whether an ID was processed.seen_chunks = {10, 20, 30}

Test your understanding

1. You need to store chat messages in order and add new messages. Which collection should you use?

Options: list / tuple / dict / set

2. You need to retrieve a model name using the key model. Which collection should you use?

Options: dict / tuple / set

3. You need to store a user's name, age, and role.

Options: list / tuple / dict / set

4. You need to remove duplicate document IDs. Which collection removes duplicate elements?

Options: list / tuple / dict / set

5. You need to store a fixed pair of image dimensions.

Options: list / tuple / dict / set

6. You must check whether an ID exists thousands of times.

Options: list / tuple / dict / set

7. What is the average-case membership complexity for a set?

Options: O(n) / O(n²) / O(1)

8. Which collection does not allow you to replace an item in place?

Options: list / tuple / dict

Show the answer

1 – list. 2 – dict. 3 – dict. 4 – set. 5 – tuple. 6 – set. 7 – O(1). 8 – tuple.

Remember these rules

  • List: ordered, editable, duplicates allowed.
  • Tuple: ordered, not editable through normal item assignment, duplicates allowed.
  • Dict: key-value pairs, unique keys.
  • Set: unique values, no indexing.
  • O(1): usually constant-time access or lookup.
  • O(n): work can grow with the number of items.

Lesson checklist

  • I can create and modify a list.
  • I can explain why a tuple is immutable.
  • I can access a dictionary value by key.
  • I can remove duplicates with a set.
  • I can explain O(1) and O(n).
  • I can select the right collection for an AI agent.

Your next step: Learn nested collections. These are important for understanding real AI agent code, JSON responses, conversation history, and RAG pipelines.

9.title: Nested Structures – Chat History and LLM Responses
9.html:
Source: Chat 11 “Python Collections Guide” (turns 1–2)

Your next step after the four collections is nested collections. They are important for understanding real AI agent code, JSON responses, conversation history, and RAG pipelines.

Python
agent = {
    "name": "Research Agent",
    "tools": ["search", "python"],
    "settings": {
        "temperature": 0.2,
        "max_steps": 5
    }
}

Here, a dictionary contains a list and another dictionary. You will see this structure frequently in real Python applications.

Question: Nested structures (chat history is a list of dicts; LLM responses are nested dicts).

A nested structure is a collection inside another collection.

For example, a dictionary can contain a list. A list can contain dictionaries. A dictionary can also contain another dictionary.

You already know the four main Python collections:

  • list stores a sequence of items.
  • tuple stores a fixed sequence of items.
  • dict stores key-value pairs.
  • set stores unique items.

Now, combine them to store real application data.

Python
user = {
    "name": "Ravi",
    "skills": ["Python", "RAG", "AI agents"]
}

Here:

  • user is a dictionary.
  • "name" has a string value.
  • "skills" has a list value.
  • The list contains three strings.

This is a nested structure.

  • user is a dict: the key "name" has the string value "Ravi"; the key "skills" has a list value that contains "Python", "RAG" and "AI agents".

The important idea is simple: each value can have its own data type, including another collection.

Chat history: a list of dictionaries

This is one of the most important nested structures for AI engineering.

An LLM conversation contains messages. Each message has a role and content.

For example:

Python
chat_history = [
    {
        "role": "user",
        "content": "What is Python?"
    },
    {
        "role": "assistant",
        "content": "Python is a programming language."
    },
    {
        "role": "user",
        "content": "What is a list?"
    }
]

Let's break it down.

  • chat_history is a list.
  • Each item in the list is a dictionary.
  • Each dictionary stores one message.
  • Each message has a "role" and "content" key.

The structure is:

  • chat_history → list
  • Index 0 → dict (role: user, content: question)
  • Index 1 → dict (role: assistant, content: answer)
  • Index 2 → dict (role: user, content: question)

How do you access nested data?

Use the list index first. Then use the dictionary key.

Python
print(chat_history[0]["role"])
print(chat_history[0]["content"])
print(chat_history[1]["content"])
Output
user
What is Python?
Python is a programming language.

Read this expression from left to right:

Python
chat_history[0]["content"]

1. chat_history selects the list.

2. [0] selects the first message.

3. ["content"] selects the message content.

You can also change a nested value:

Python
chat_history[0]["content"] = "Explain Python."

You do not need to rebuild the entire list. You can change the value inside the dictionary.

How do you add a message?

Use append() to add a new dictionary to the list.

Python
chat_history.append({
    "role": "assistant",
    "content": "A list stores multiple items."
})

Now the list contains four messages.

AI engineering connection: Chat history is often passed to an LLM so that it can use previous messages as context. The exact message format depends on the API or framework.

LLM responses: nested dictionaries

An LLM API can return a complex response. The response can contain dictionaries inside dictionaries and lists inside dictionaries.

Here is a simplified example:

Python
response = {
    "id": "resp_123",
    "model": "example-model",
    "output": [
        {
            "type": "message",
            "role": "assistant",
            "content": [
                {
                    "type": "output_text",
                    "text": "Python uses indentation."
                }
            ]
        }
    ]
}

This is sample data for learning. It is not a complete response from a specific provider.

Notice the structure:

  • response is a dictionary.
  • "output" contains a list.
  • The list contains a dictionary.
  • "content" contains another list.
  • The inner list contains a dictionary with the text.

To retrieve the generated text, follow the structure one level at a time.

Python
answer = response["output"][0]["content"][0]["text"]

print(answer)
Output
Python uses indentation.

Let's read the expression:

ExpressionMeaning
response["output"]Get the output list
[0]Get the first output item
["content"]Get its content list
[0]Get the first content item
["text"]Get the generated text

You can use the same method with API responses, tool calls, RAG results, and agent state.

How do you process nested structures?

You will often need to process every message in a conversation.

Use a for loop.

Python
for message in chat_history:
    print(message["role"])
    print(message["content"])

Here, message represents one dictionary at a time.

The loop does not need to know how many messages exist. It processes each message in the list.

Example: Get only user messages

Python
for message in chat_history:
    if message["role"] == "user":
        print(message["content"])

This is useful when you need to inspect user questions or analyze a conversation.

Example: Process a list of retrieved documents

A RAG system may return a list of dictionaries:

Python
documents = [
    {"text": "Python is easy to learn.", "score": 0.95},
    {"text": "Python supports dictionaries.", "score": 0.88},
    {"text": "Python supports lists.", "score": 0.82}
]

for document in documents:
    print(document["text"])
    print(document["score"])

Each document has text and a retrieval score. You can access both values by using dictionary keys.

Avoid common errors

Error 1: Using the wrong index

Python
print(chat_history[10]["content"])

This raises an IndexError if the list has fewer than 11 items.

Check the list length when the index is not known:

Python
if len(chat_history) > 10:
    print(chat_history[10]["content"])

Error 2: Using a key that does not exist

Python
print(chat_history[0]["timestamp"])

This raises a KeyError if the first message has no "timestamp" key.

Use get() when the key may be missing:

Python
print(chat_history[0].get("timestamp", "Not available"))

Error 3: Assuming every item has the same structure

Real API responses can contain different output types. Some items may contain text. Others may contain tool calls or other data.

Do not assume every nested item has a "text" key. Check the structure first.

Python
for item in response["output"]:
    if item.get("type") == "message":
        print(item["role"])

This checks the output type before it processes the message.

Practice: Read nested data

First, read this code:

Python
orders = [
    {"item": "Keyboard", "total": 1500},
    {"item": "Mouse", "total": 700}
]

1. What is the type of orders?

Options: dict / list / str

2. How do you get the first order's total?

Options: orders[0]['total'] / orders['total'][0] / orders.total[0]

3. How do you add a new order?

Options: orders.add({...}) / orders.append({...}) / orders[0]({...})

Show the answer

1 – list. 2 – orders[0]['total']. 3 – orders.append({...}).

Remember these rules

TaskWhat to use
Store multiple messagesList
Store the fields of one messageDictionary
Read a messagechat_history[0]
Read its contentchat_history[0]["content"]
Add a messagechat_history.append({...})
Read nested LLM outputFollow each key and index
Handle an optional keymessage.get("key")
Process every messagefor loop

The key skill: Read the data structure from the outside to the inside. At each level, identify whether you have a list, dictionary, or another collection. Then select the next item or key.

This is an essential skill for reading Python code that uses LLM APIs, RAG pipelines, and AI agents.
